Recalibrate the credible intervals of ABC with random forests

Source: R/abc.R
abc_calibrate.Rd

Measures, on simulations that were not used to fit, where the true value of each parameter falls in its estimated posterior, and uses this to correct the credible intervals of predict(). For each simulation of pseudo, the probability integral transform (PIT) is the posterior distribution function at the true value, read from 999 quantiles of the quantile regression forest. If the intervals were calibrated, the PIT would be uniform between 0 and 1 (Prangle et al. 2014); intervals that are too wide give PIT values crowded in the middle, and intervals that are too narrow give values crowded at the ends. With calibration, predict() then asks the forest for the quantiles of the PIT instead of the nominal probabilities: for a level of 0.9, the 5% and 95% quantiles of the PIT values, so that 90% of the calibration simulations would fall inside.

Usage

abc_calibrate(fit, pseudo, ncores = 1)

Arguments

fit

An mc_abc_fit from abc_fit().

pseudo

Data frame of simulations from the same prior and model that were not used to fit, with the parameters and statistics of fit (for example a second abc_table() with another seed). Rows with missing or infinite values are dropped; at least 20 must remain. A few hundred give quantiles of the PIT precise enough for a 90% interval.

ncores

Number of threads for the forests. One whole number, 1 or more.

Value

An mc_abc_calibration: a list with pit (one vector per parameter), coverage (a data frame with the fraction of simulations of pseudo inside the nominal 50%, 80%, 90% and 95% intervals of each parameter, before recalibration) and n, the number of simulations used.

Details

This is a global version of the recalibration of Rodrigues et al. (2018), who weight the calibration simulations by their closeness to the observation. It corrects the coverage on average over the prior, as measured by abc_recovery(), and not the interval of one observation, which can still be too wide or too narrow where the posterior differs from the average. It cannot make an uninformative posterior informative either: for a parameter that the statistics do not inform, the PIT is already about uniform and nothing changes. Nor can it widen an interval beyond the parameters of the simulations that share leaves with the observation: with one statistic and the default min_node_size, the truth fell outside all of them in about 13% of the simulations, so recalibrated 90% and 95% intervals both held it in about 87% (data-raw/abc_recalibration.R); a larger min_node_size of abc_fit() is the remedy there.

References

Prangle, D., Blum, M. G. B., Popovic, G., & Sisson, S. A. (2014). Diagnostic tools for approximate Bayesian computation using the coverage property. Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics, 56, 309–329. doi:10.1111/anzs.12087

Rodrigues, G. S., Prangle, D., & Sisson, S. A. (2018). Recalibration: A post-processing method for approximate Bayesian computation. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 126, 53–66. doi:10.1016/j.csda.2018.04.004

See also

Other inference: abc_choose(), abc_cv(), abc_diagnose(), abc_fit(), abc_ppc(), abc_recovery(), abc_table(), fold_summarise(), nobs.mc_node_test(), observe_detection(), plot.mc_abc_choice(), plot.mc_abc_fit(), spatial_folds()

Examples

set.seed(1)
make <- function(n) {
  d <- data.frame(a = runif(n))
  d$s <- d$a + rnorm(n, 0, 0.05)
  d
}
fit <- abc_fit(make(1000), parameters = "a", ntree = 100)
#> abc_fit() implements the method of:
#>   Raynal, L., Marin, J.-M., Pudlo, P., Ribatet, M., Robert, C. P., & Estoup, A. (2019). ABC random forests for Bayesian parameter inference. Bioinformatics, 35, 1720-1728. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty867
#> Please cite these papers together with comdynamite (citation("comdynamite")).
#> This message is shown once per session; options(comdynamite.cite = FALSE) turns it off.
calibration <- abc_calibrate(fit, make(200))
calibration$coverage
#>   parameter level coverage
#> 1         a  0.50    0.375
#> 2         a  0.80    0.600
#> 3         a  0.90    0.650
#> 4         a  0.95    0.730
predict(fit, c(s = 0.5), calibration = calibration)
#>   observation parameter  estimate       low      high      mean
#> 1           1         a 0.4934904 0.4349082 0.5394022 0.4883662
